context_stem: To facilitate the effective implementation of this policy across the company, we commit to the following:
excerpt: Responsible Scaling Officer: We will maintain the position of Responsible Scaling Officer, a designated member of staff who is responsible for reducing catastrophic risk, primarily by ensuring this policy is designed and implemented effectively.
paraphrase: Anthropic commits to maintaining a Responsible Scaling Officer role responsible for reducing catastrophic risk through effective policy design and implementation.

excerpt: The Responsible Scaling Officer's duties will include (but are not limited to): (1) as needed, proposing updates to this policy to the Board of Directors; (2) approving relevant model training or deployment decisions based on capability and safeguard assessments;
paraphrase: The RSO's duties include proposing policy updates and approving training/deployment decisions based on assessments.

excerpt: (3) reviewing major contracts (i.e., deployment partnerships) for consistency with this policy; (4) overseeing implementation of this policy, including the allocation of sufficient resources; (5) receiving and addressing reports of potential instances of noncompliance;
paraphrase: The RSO's duties also include reviewing major contracts, overseeing implementation and resource allocation, and handling noncompliance reports.

excerpt: (6) promptly notifying the Board of Directors of any cases of noncompliance that pose material risk; and (7) making judgment calls on policy interpretation and application.
paraphrase: The RSO's final duties are notifying the Board of material noncompliance and making interpretive judgment calls.

excerpt: Readiness: We will develop internal safety procedures for incident scenarios. Such scenarios include (1) pausing training in response to reaching Capability Thresholds; (2) responding to a security incident involving model weights; and (3) responding to severe jailbreaks or vulnerabilities in deployed models, including restricting access in safety emergencies that cannot otherwise be mitigated.
paraphrase: Anthropic will develop internal procedures covering incident scenarios such as training pauses, security incidents, and severe jailbreaks.

excerpt: We will run exercises to ensure our readiness for incident scenarios.
paraphrase: Anthropic will conduct exercises to test readiness for incident scenarios.

excerpt: Transparency: We will share summaries of Capability Reports and Safeguards Reports with Anthropic's regular-clearance staff, redacting any highly-sensitive information.
paraphrase: Anthropic will share redacted report summaries with regular-clearance staff.

excerpt: We will share a minimally redacted version of these reports with a subset of staff, to help us surface relevant technical safety considerations.
paraphrase: A minimally redacted version of the reports will go to a subset of staff to surface technical safety issues.

excerpt: Internal review: For each Capabilities or Safeguards Report, we will solicit feedback from internal teams with visibility into the relevant activities, with the aims of informing future refinements to our methodology and, in some circumstances, identifying weaknesses and informing the CEO and RSO's decisions.
paraphrase: For each report, Anthropic will solicit internal team feedback to refine methodology and inform leadership decisions.

excerpt: Noncompliance: We will maintain a process through which Anthropic staff may anonymously notify the Responsible Scaling Officer of any potential instances of noncompliance with this policy.
paraphrase: Anthropic will maintain an anonymous reporting process for noncompliance to the RSO.

excerpt: We will also establish a policy governing noncompliance reporting, which will (1) protect reporters from retaliation and (2) set forth a mechanism for escalating reports to one or more members of the Board of Directors in cases where the report relates to conduct of the Responsible Scaling Officer.
paraphrase: Anthropic will establish a reporting policy that protects reporters and provides escalation to the Board for reports about the RSO.

excerpt: Further, we will track and investigate any reported or otherwise identified potential instances of noncompliance with this policy.
paraphrase: Anthropic will track and investigate all identified noncompliance instances.

excerpt: Where reports are substantiated, we will take appropriate and proportional corrective action and document the same.
paraphrase: Substantiated reports will result in proportional corrective action, documented accordingly.

excerpt: The Responsible Scaling Officer will regularly update the Board of Directors on substantial cases of noncompliance and overall trends.
paraphrase: The RSO will regularly brief the Board on major noncompliance cases and trends.

excerpt: In addition to noncompliance processes, we will (1) establish pathways for Anthropic staff to raise any issues related to this policy, including the overall risk levels of our models and implementation challenges; and (2) regularly review our compliance with this policy's procedural requirements.
paraphrase: Beyond noncompliance channels, Anthropic will create issue-raising pathways and conduct regular compliance reviews.

excerpt: Cases deemed to present minimal additional risk may be reported to the Board in quarterly summary reports.
paraphrase: Low-risk cases can be reported to the Board via quarterly summaries instead of individually.

excerpt: In cases where this policy is unintentionally ambiguous, we will act in accordance with the Responsible Scaling Officer or CEO's judgment, and aim to clarify the ambiguity in the next policy update.
paraphrase: Ambiguities will be resolved via RSO or CEO judgment, with clarification intended in a subsequent update.

excerpt: Employee agreements: We will not impose contractual non-disparagement obligations on employees, candidates, or former employees in a way that could impede or discourage them from publicly raising safety concerns about Anthropic.
paraphrase: Anthropic will not use non-disparagement clauses to discourage employees from raising safety concerns.

excerpt: If we offer agreements with a non-disparagement clause, that clause will not preclude raising safety concerns, nor will it preclude disclosure of the existence of that clause.
paraphrase: Any non-disparagement clause offered will not block safety-concern disclosure or disclosure of the clause itself.

excerpt: Policy changes: Changes to this policy will be proposed by the CEO and the Responsible Scaling Officer and approved by the Board of Directors, in consultation with the Long-Term Benefit Trust.
paraphrase: Policy changes are proposed by the CEO and RSO and approved by the Board with LTBT consultation.

excerpt: The current version of the RSP is accessible at www.anthropic.com/rsp. We will update the public version of the RSP before any changes take effect and record any differences from the prior draft in a change log.
paraphrase: The current RSP is published online, and any changes will be publicly updated before taking effect with differences logged.

context_stem: To advance the public dialogue on the regulation of frontier AI model risks and to enable examination of our actions, we commit to the following:
excerpt: Public disclosures: We will publicly release key information related to the evaluation and deployment of our models (not including sensitive details). These include summaries of related Capability and Safeguards reports when we deploy a model as well as plans for current and future comprehensive capability assessments and deployment and security safeguards.
paraphrase: Anthropic will publicly release non-sensitive information including report summaries at deployment and plans for capability assessments and safeguards.

excerpt: We will also periodically release information on internal reports of potential instances of non-compliance and other implementation challenges we encounter.
paraphrase: Anthropic will periodically release information about internal noncompliance reports and implementation challenges.

excerpt: Expert input: We will solicit input from external experts in relevant domains in the process of developing and conducting capability and safeguards assessments.
paraphrase: Anthropic will solicit external expert input during development and conduct of capability and safeguards assessments.

excerpt: We may also solicit external expert input prior to making final decisions on the capability and safeguards assessments.
paraphrase: Anthropic may also seek external expert input before finalizing assessment decisions.

excerpt: U.S. Government notice: We will notify a relevant U.S. Government entity if a model requires stronger protections than the ASL-2 Standard.
paraphrase: Anthropic will notify a relevant U.S. Government entity if a model needs protections beyond ASL-2.

excerpt: Procedural compliance review: On approximately an annual basis, we will commission a third-party review that assesses whether we adhered to this policy's main procedural commitments (we expect to iterate on the exact list since this has not been done before for RSPs).
paraphrase: Anthropic will commission an annual third-party review of adherence to procedural commitments, expecting to refine the review's scope over time.

excerpt: This review will focus on procedural compliance, not substantive outcomes. We will also do such reviews internally on a more regular cadence.
paraphrase: The third-party review focuses on procedure not outcomes, and internal reviews will occur more frequently.

excerpt: It is possible at some point in the future that another actor in the frontier AI ecosystem will pass, or be on track to imminently pass, a Capability Threshold without implementing measures equivalent to the Required Safeguards such that their actions pose a serious risk for the world.
paraphrase: The footnote considers a future scenario where another AI actor exceeds a Capability Threshold without equivalent safeguards, posing serious world risk.

excerpt: In such a scenario, because the incremental increase in risk attributable to us would be small, we might decide to lower the Required Safeguards.
paraphrase: In that scenario, Anthropic might lower Required Safeguards since its own incremental risk contribution would be small.

excerpt: If we take this measure, however, we will also acknowledge the overall level of risk posed by AI systems (including ours), and will invest significantly in making a case to the U.S. government for taking regulatory action to mitigate such risk to acceptable levels.
paraphrase: If safeguards are lowered under this scenario, Anthropic will acknowledge overall AI risk and advocate for U.S. government regulatory action.

excerpt: We currently expect that if we do not deploy the model publicly and instead proceed with training or limited deployments, we will likely instead share evaluation details with a relevant U.S. Government entity.
paraphrase: For non-public deployments, Anthropic expects to share evaluation details with a relevant U.S. Government entity instead.

excerpt: These will be posted to www.anthropic.com/rsp-updates. We anticipate providing updates at least every 6-12 months.
paraphrase: Updates will be posted online, expected at least every 6-12 months.

excerpt: Where possible, we will include descriptions of the empirical evaluation results we believe would indicate that a model is no longer safe to store under the ASL-2 Standard.
paraphrase: Where feasible, updates will describe evaluation results indicating a model is no longer safe under ASL-2.

excerpt: Our purpose in these updates is to provide sufficient detail to facilitate conversations about best practices for safeguards, capability evaluations, and elicitation.
paraphrase: The purpose of the updates is to enable dialogue on best practices for safeguards, evaluations, and elicitation.

excerpt: Technical and operational standards for safely training and deploying frontier AI models. Higher ASLs correspond to stronger safety and security measures required for more capable models.
paraphrase: ASLs are graded standards for safe training and deployment, with higher levels requiring stronger measures.

excerpt: The current default standard for all Anthropic models, including security measures, safety testing, and automated misuse detection.
paraphrase: ASL-2 is the default standard for all models covering security, safety testing, and misuse detection.

excerpt: A higher level of safeguards required when a model cannot be certified as ASL-2 appropriate. It includes more stringent security and deployment measures designed to mitigate risks from more capable models.
paraphrase: ASL-3 is a stronger safeguard tier for models that no longer qualify as ASL-2 appropriate.

excerpt: A document attesting that a model is sufficiently far from each of the relevant Capability Thresholds, and therefore (still) appropriate for storing under an ASL-N Standard. It includes evaluation procedures, results, and other relevant evidence gathered around the time of testing.
paraphrase: A Capability Report documents that a model remains sufficiently distant from relevant Capability Thresholds, including evaluation evidence.

excerpt: Specific AI capabilities that, if reached, would require stronger safeguards than the current baseline ASL-N standard provides.
paraphrase: Capability Thresholds are specific capabilities that trigger the need for stronger safeguards.

excerpt: A scaling trend-based metric that accounts for both FLOPs and algorithmic improvements.
paraphrase: Effective Compute is a metric combining raw compute and algorithmic efficiency gains.

excerpt: Empirical tests designed to provide early warning when a model is approaching a Capability Threshold. These tests are intended to trigger before a model actually reaches a dangerous capability.
paraphrase: Evaluations are empirical tests meant to warn before a model reaches a dangerous capability.

excerpt: Floating-Point Operation(s). The amount of computation required to train or run a model. The number of FLOPs can be used as one indicator of a model's computational complexity and, indirectly, its potential capabilities.
paraphrase: FLOPs measure computation used to train or run a model and serve as an indirect capability indicator.

excerpt: Anthropic's Board of Directors approves the RSP and receives Capability Reports and Safeguards Reports. The LTBT is an external body that is consulted on policy changes and also provided with Capability Reports and Safeguards Reports.
paraphrase: The Board approves the RSP and receives reports; the LTBT is an external body consulted on changes and also receiving reports.

excerpt: The standard of safety and security measures that must be implemented when a model reaches a Capability Threshold.
paraphrase: Required Safeguards are the mandated measures triggered when a Capability Threshold is reached.

excerpt: A designated staff member responsible for reducing catastrophic risk, primarily by ensuring this policy is designed and implemented effectively. Their duties include reviewing policy updates, approving reports, overseeing implementation, and approving deployments.
paraphrase: The RSO is the staff member tasked with reducing catastrophic risk via policy design/implementation, report approval, and deployment sign-off.

excerpt: A document attesting that the implemented safeguards meet an ASL-N Standard. It details the design and planned implementation of safeguards, and evidence to demonstrate their expected effectiveness.
paraphrase: A Safeguards Report attests that safeguards meet an ASL-N standard, detailing design and evidence of effectiveness.

excerpt: Acceptable use policies and model cards: Publication of model cards for significant new models describing capabilities, limitations, evaluations, and intended use cases.
paraphrase: ASL-2 deployment requires publishing model cards describing capabilities, limitations, evaluations, and intended uses.

excerpt: Enforcement of a Usage Policy that restricts, at a minimum, catastrophic and high harm use cases, including using the model to generate content that could cause severe risks to the continued existence of humankind, or direct and severe harm to individuals.
paraphrase: A Usage Policy is enforced restricting catastrophic and high-harm use cases including existential and severe individual harm content.

excerpt: Harmlessness training and automated detection: Training models to refuse requests to aid in causing harm, such as with Constitutional AI or other improved techniques, and the use of model enhanced trust and safety detection and enforcement.
paraphrase: Models are trained to refuse harmful requests using techniques like Constitutional AI, alongside enhanced trust and safety detection.

excerpt: Fine-tuning protections: In finetuning products, data is filtered for harmfulness, and models are subject to automated evaluation to check harmlessness features are not degraded.
paraphrase: Finetuning products filter harmful data and undergo automated checks to ensure harmlessness features remain intact.

excerpt: There are a very limited number of use cases where this tooling is disabled. These are negotiated on a case by case basis and considered only for extremely low risk use cases that involve company personnel.
paraphrase: Disabling this tooling is limited to rare, individually negotiated, extremely low-risk cases involving company personnel.

excerpt: Vulnerability reporting channels: Clearly indicated paths within the product for users to report harmful or dangerous model outputs, as well as a bug bounty for universal jailbreaks.
paraphrase: Products provide clear reporting paths for harmful outputs and a bug bounty targeting universal jailbreaks.

excerpt: ASL-2 Security Standard: A security system that can likely thwart most opportunistic attackers.
paraphrase: The ASL-2 Security Standard is designed to likely thwart most opportunistic attackers.

excerpt: Supply chain: Vendor and supplier security must be regularly reviewed to ensure that they meet security standards. Software updates should be frequently managed and compliance monitoring automated where possible.
paraphrase: Vendor/supplier security must be regularly reviewed, with frequent software updates and automated compliance monitoring where feasible.

excerpt: Offices: Physical security should entail visitor access logs and restrictions protect on-site assets. Highly sensitive interactions should utilize advanced authentication like security keys.
paraphrase: Physical office security should include visitor logs and access restrictions, with advanced authentication like security keys for sensitive interactions.

excerpt: Network visibility should be maintained and office access controls and communications should maximize on-site protections.
paraphrase: Network visibility and office access controls should be maintained to maximize on-site protection.

excerpt: Workforce: People-critical processes must represent a key aspect of cybersecurity. Mandatory periodic infosec training educates all employees on secure practices, like proper system configurations and strong passwords, and fosters a proactive "security mindset."
paraphrase: Workforce security requires mandatory periodic infosec training covering secure practices and fostering a security mindset.

excerpt: Fundamental infrastructure and policies promoting secure-by-design and secure-by-default principles should be incorporated into the engineering process. An insider risk program should tie access to job roles. Rapid incident response protocols must be deployed.
paraphrase: Secure-by-design principles should be built into engineering, an insider risk program should tie access to roles, and rapid incident response must be deployed.

excerpt: Compartmentalization: Segmented system isolation must ensure limited blast radius. Features like zero trust architecture should require access from approved devices.
paraphrase: System isolation must limit blast radius, and zero trust architecture should restrict access to approved devices.

excerpt: Strict protocols must be deployed to regulate weight copies on company networks and limit storage to only approved, restricted systems.
paraphrase: Strict protocols must regulate weight copies and restrict storage to approved systems.

excerpt: Infrastructure: Standard security infrastructure, monitoring software, access management tools, and disk encryption provide a technology baseline.
paraphrase: A technology baseline includes standard security infrastructure, monitoring, access management, and disk encryption.

excerpt: Process elements like incident reporting procedures, lost/stolen device protocols and Detection and Response should support these. External validation like SOC 2 compliance and continuous vulnerability management must ensure adaptations match infosec developments.
paraphrase: Supporting processes include incident reporting, device loss protocols, and Detection and Response, alongside SOC 2 validation and vulnerability management.

excerpt: Programs like bug bounties and vulnerability discovery should incentivize exposing flaws.
paraphrase: Bug bounty and vulnerability discovery programs should incentivize flaw exposure.

excerpt: Operations: Ongoing configuration management, compliance drills, integrated security approaches and mandatory external reviews should embed security within regular operations and harden processes during organizational changes.
paraphrase: Operations should embed security through configuration management, compliance drills, integrated approaches, and mandatory external reviews, including during organizational change.

excerpt: This appendix contains detailed definitions for each Capability Threshold in Section 2.
paraphrase: The appendix provides detailed definitions for the Capability Thresholds referenced in Section 2.

context_stem: Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) weapons:
excerpt: CBRN-3: The ability to significantly assist individuals or groups with basic STEM backgrounds in obtaining, producing, or deploying CBRN weapons.
paraphrase: CBRN-3 is defined as the ability to significantly assist STEM-literate individuals or groups in obtaining, producing, or deploying CBRN weapons.

excerpt: We assess this by comparing what potential attackers could achieve with full model access versus 2023-level online resources, assuming they have funding and up to one year of time to invest, but no initial specialized expertise.
paraphrase: CBRN-3 is assessed by comparing attacker capability with full model access versus 2023-level resources, given funding and up to one year, without prior specialized expertise.

context_stem: Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) weapons:
excerpt: CBRN-4: The ability to substantially uplift CBRN developmentcapabilities of moderately resourced state programs (with relevant expert teams), such as by novel weapons design, substantially accelerating existing processes, or dramatic reduction in technical barriers.
paraphrase: CBRN-4 is the ability to substantially uplift moderately resourced state CBRN programs via novel design, acceleration, or reduced technical barriers.

excerpt: We currently define this as uplifting a team of people with skills equivalent to entry-level PhD biologists to be able to approximate the capabilities of a world-class, state-backed bioweapons team.
paraphrase: CBRN-4 is currently defined as enabling entry-level PhD-equivalent teams to approximate world-class state-backed bioweapons capabilities.
stated_bar: entry-level PhD biologists to world-class state-backed team

excerpt: AI R&D-4: The ability to fully automate the work of an entry-level, remote-only Researcher at Anthropic.
paraphrase: AI R&D-4 is defined as the ability to fully automate an entry-level remote researcher's work at Anthropic.

excerpt: AI R&D-5: The ability to cause dramatic acceleration in the rate of effective scaling. Specifically, this would be the case if we observed or projected an increase in the effective training compute of the world's most capable model that, over the course of a year, was equivalent to two years of the average rate of progress during the period of early 2018 to early 2024.
paraphrase: AI R&D-5 is defined as capability causing a one-year increase in effective training compute equal to two years of 2018-2024 average progress.

excerpt: We roughly estimate that the 2018-2024 average scaleup was around 35x per year, so this would imply an actual or projected one-year scaleup of 352 = ~1000x.
paraphrase: The estimated average scaleup of ~35x per year implies a threshold one-year scaleup of roughly 1000x.

excerpt: Model Autonomy checkpoint: The ability to perform a wide range of advanced software engineering tasks autonomously that could be precursors to full autonomous replication or automated AI R&D, and that would take a domain expert human 2-8 hours to complete.
paraphrase: The Model Autonomy checkpoint covers autonomous performance of advanced software engineering tasks taking a human expert 2-8 hours, as precursors to full autonomy.

excerpt: We primarily view this level of model autonomy as a checkpoint on the way to managing the risks of robust, fully autonomous systems with capabilities that might include (a) automating and greatly accelerating research and development in AI development (b) generating their own revenue and using it to run copies of themselves in large-scale, hard-to-shut-down operations.
paraphrase: This checkpoint is viewed as a step toward managing fully autonomous systems capable of self-directed R&D acceleration or self-funded, hard-to-shut-down replication.

excerpt: We are uncertain how to choose a specific threshold, but we maintain a current list of specific CBRN capabilities of concern for which we would implement stronger mitigations.
paraphrase: Anthropic acknowledges uncertainty in threshold-setting but maintains a list of specific concerning CBRN capabilities warranting stronger mitigations.

excerpt: We treat these lists as sensitive, but we plan to share them with organizations such as AI Safety Institutes and the Frontier Model Forum, and keep these lists updated.
paraphrase: These sensitive lists are planned to be shared with bodies like AI Safety Institutes and the Frontier Model Forum, and kept current.

excerpt: This comparison is hard to make in practice; this note is to clarify the meaning of the conceptual threshold and the fact that this policy aims to measure risk relative to the world in 2023, so that we can understand how much risk the current generations of frontier models are creating.
paraphrase: The footnote clarifies that comparisons are conceptually difficult, and risk is measured relative to a 2023 baseline to gauge current model risk contribution.

excerpt: The 35x/year scaleup estimate is based on assuming the rate of increase in compute being used to train frontier models from ~2018 to May 2024 is 4.2x/year (reference), the impact of increased (LLM) algorithmic efficiency is roughly equivalent to a further 2.8x/year (reference), and the impact of post training enhancements is a further 3x/year (informal estimate).
paraphrase: The 35x/year figure derives from combining 4.2x/year compute growth, 2.8x/year algorithmic efficiency gains, and 3x/year post-training enhancement gains.

excerpt: Combined, these have an effective rate of scaling of 35x/year.
paraphrase: Combining the compute, algorithmic, and post-training factors yields an effective scaling rate of 35x/year.

excerpt: September 19, 2023 (RSP v1.0) RSP-2023 (aka RSP v1.0): Initial version.
paraphrase: The changelog records that the initial RSP version 1.0 was released on September 19, 2023.

excerpt: RSP-2024: This update introduces a more flexible and nuanced approach to assessing and managing AI risks while maintaining our commitment not to train or deploy models unless we have implemented adequate safeguards.
paraphrase: The 2024 update introduces a more flexible risk management approach while preserving the commitment not to train/deploy without adequate safeguards.

excerpt: Key improvements include new capability thresholds to indicate when we should upgrade our safeguards, refined processes for evaluating model capabilities and the adequacy of our safeguards (inspired by safety case methodologies), and new measures for internal governance and external input.
paraphrase: Key improvements include new capability thresholds, refined evaluation processes inspired by safety cases, and new governance and external input measures.

excerpt: ASL definition changed: The term "ASL" now refers to groups of technical and operational safeguards (it previously also referred to models). We also introduced the new concepts of Capability Thresholds and Required Safeguards.
paraphrase: The changelog notes ASL now refers only to safeguard groups, not models, alongside new Capability Thresholds and Required Safeguards concepts.

excerpt: This change allows for more targeted application of safeguards based on specific capabilities, rather than broad model categories.
paraphrase: The redefinition enables targeting safeguards to specific capabilities instead of broad model categories.

locator: Changelog / v2.0 / ARA threshold now a checkpoint
excerpt: ARA threshold now a checkpoint: We replaced our previous autonomous replication and adaption (ARA) threshold with a "checkpoint" for autonomous AI capabilities.
paraphrase: The ARA threshold was replaced with a checkpoint concept for autonomous AI capabilities.

locator: Changelog / v2.0 / ARA threshold now a checkpoint
excerpt: Rather than triggering higher safety standards automatically, reaching this checkpoint will prompt additional evaluation of the model's capabilities and accelerate our preparation of stronger safeguards.
paraphrase: Reaching the checkpoint prompts additional evaluation and faster safeguard preparation rather than automatic standard escalation.

locator: Changelog / v2.0 / ARA threshold now a checkpoint
excerpt: We previously considered these capabilities as a trigger for increased safeguards, motivated by an attempt to establish some threshold while we developed a better sense of potential threats.
paraphrase: Previously these capabilities triggered increased safeguards as a provisional threshold while understanding of threats matured.

locator: Changelog / v2.0 / ARA threshold now a checkpoint
excerpt: We now believe that these capabilities - at the levels we initially considered - would not necessitate the ASL-3 standard.
paraphrase: Anthropic now believes those originally considered capability levels do not require the ASL-3 standard.

locator: Changelog / v2.0 / AI R&D threshold added
excerpt: AI R&D threshold added: We added a new threshold for AI systems that can significantly advance AI development.
paraphrase: A new threshold was added for AI systems capable of significantly advancing AI development.

locator: Changelog / v2.0 / AI R&D threshold added
excerpt: Such capabilities could lead to rapid, unpredictable advances in AI, potentially outpacing our ability to evaluate and address emerging risks, and may also serve as an early warning sign for the ability to automate R&D in other domains.
paraphrase: These capabilities risk rapid unpredictable AI advances outpacing risk evaluation, and could signal broader R&D automation ability.

locator: Changelog / v2.0 / Testing for Capability Thresholds
excerpt: Testing for Capability Thresholds: Rather than using prespecified evaluations, we now require an affirmative case that models are sufficiently far from Capability Thresholds.
paraphrase: Instead of prespecified evaluations, Anthropic now requires an affirmative case that models are sufficiently distant from Capability Thresholds.

locator: Changelog / v2.0 / Testing for Capability Thresholds
excerpt: Predefined tests may miss emerging risks or be overly conservative relative to the actual threshold of concern.
paraphrase: Predefined tests risk missing emerging risks or being overly conservative relative to the true threshold.

locator: Changelog / v2.0 / Testing for Capability Thresholds
excerpt: Our most accurate tests change frequently enough that it is more practical to use this new approach than to have our Board of Directors pre-approve evaluations.
paraphrase: Because accurate tests evolve rapidly, this new approach is more practical than requiring Board pre-approval of evaluations.

excerpt: Adjusted evaluation cadence: We adjusted the comprehensive assessment cadence to 4x Effective Compute or six months of accumulated post-training enhancements (this was previously three months).
paraphrase: The evaluation cadence changed to 4x Effective Compute or six months of post-training enhancement accumulation, up from three months.
stated_bar: 4x Effective Compute or six months (previously three months)

excerpt: We found that a three-month cadence forced teams to prioritize conducting frequent evaluations over more comprehensive testing and improving methodologies.
paraphrase: The prior three-month cadence forced prioritizing frequency over comprehensiveness and methodology improvement.

locator: Changelog / v2.0 / Less prescriptive evaluation methodology
excerpt: Less prescriptive evaluation methodology: We have replaced some specifics in our previous testing methodology (e.g., using 1% of compute for elicitation or creating a 6x buffer), with more general requirements to (a) match expected efforts of potential adversaries and (b) provide informal estimates of how further scaling and research developments will impact model capabilities and performance on the same tasks.
paraphrase: Specific prior methodology details (1% compute, 6x buffer) were replaced with general requirements to match adversary efforts and estimate future scaling impact.

locator: Changelog / v2.0 / Less prescriptive evaluation methodology
excerpt: We have found that specific methodologies may become outdated when new research developments are introduced.
paraphrase: Specific methodologies risk becoming outdated as new research emerges.

locator: Changelog / v2.0 / Less prescriptive evaluation methodology
excerpt: Although still an aspirational goal, the science of evaluations is not currently mature enough to make confident predictions about the precise buffer we should require between current models and a Capability Threshold.
paraphrase: Precise buffer requirements remain an aspirational goal, since evaluation science is not yet mature enough for confident predictions.

locator: Changelog / v2.0 / More outcome-focused safeguard requirements
excerpt: More outcome-focused safeguard requirements: We have updated our ASL-3 safeguards requirements to be less prescriptive and more outcome-focused.
paraphrase: ASL-3 safeguard requirements were updated to be more outcome-focused and less prescriptive.

locator: Changelog / v2.0 / More outcome-focused safeguard requirements
excerpt: Rather than detailing specific operational and technical safeguards, we now specify the overall security or deployment standards and requirements for meeting them.
paraphrase: Instead of detailing specific safeguards, overall standards and requirements for meeting them are now specified.

locator: Changelog / v2.0 / More outcome-focused safeguard requirements
excerpt: This is to allow us to adapt our safeguards more flexibly as our understanding of risks and possible safeguards improves.
paraphrase: The change allows more flexible safeguard adaptation as risk and safeguard understanding evolves.

locator: Changelog / v2.0 / Clarified ASL-3 and ASL-2 security threat models
excerpt: Clarified ASL-3 and ASL-2 security threat models: We have clarified which actors are in and out of scope for the ASL-3 Security Standard.
paraphrase: The update clarifies which threat actors are in or out of scope for the ASL-3 Security Standard.

locator: Changelog / v2.0 / Clarified ASL-3 and ASL-2 security threat models
excerpt: We also removed the commitment to protect against scaled attacks and distillation attacks from the ASL-2 Security standard.
paraphrase: The commitment to protect against scaled and distillation attacks was removed from the ASL-2 Security standard.

locator: Changelog / v2.0 / Clarified ASL-3 and ASL-2 security threat models
excerpt: While distillation remains a concern for more capable models, models stored under ASL-2 safeguards have not yet reached potentially harmful Capability Thresholds.
paraphrase: Distillation is still a concern for more capable models, but ASL-2 models have not reached harmful Capability Thresholds.

locator: Changelog / v2.0 / Clarified requirements for deployments with trusted users
excerpt: Clarified requirements for deployments with trusted users: We have updated the ASL-3 Deployment Standard to allow for different levels of safeguards based on deployment context.
paraphrase: The ASL-3 Deployment Standard now allows different safeguard levels depending on deployment context.

locator: Changelog / v2.0 / Clarified requirements for deployments with trusted users
excerpt: For any general access systems, we still require passing intensive red-teaming.
paraphrase: General access systems still require passing intensive red-teaming.

locator: Changelog / v2.0 / Clarified requirements for deployments with trusted users
excerpt: For internal use, safety testing and deployments to sufficiently trusted users, we will instead require a combination of access controls and monitoring.
paraphrase: For internal use, safety testing, and trusted-user deployments, access controls and monitoring will be required instead.

locator: Changelog / v2.0 / New Capability and Safeguards Reports
excerpt: New Capability and Safeguards Reports: We have introduced Capability Reports and Safeguard Reports.
paraphrase: Capability Reports and Safeguard Reports were newly introduced.

locator: Changelog / v2.0 / New Capability and Safeguards Reports
excerpt: We expect that aggregating all the available evidence about model capabilities will provide decision makers with a more complete picture of the overall level of risk and improve our ability to solicit feedback on our work.
paraphrase: Aggregating capability evidence is expected to give decision-makers a fuller risk picture and improve feedback solicitation.

locator: Changelog / v2.0 / Internal and external accountability
excerpt: Internal and external accountability: We have made a number of changes to our previous "procedural commitments." These include expanding the duties of the Responsible Scaling Officer; adding internal critique and external expert input on capability and safeguard assessments;
paraphrase: Procedural commitment changes include expanded RSO duties and added internal critique plus external expert input on assessments.

locator: Changelog / v2.0 / Internal and external accountability
excerpt: new procedures related to internal governance; and maintaining a public page for overviews of past Capability and Safeguard Reports, RSP-related updates, and future plans.
paraphrase: Additional changes include new internal governance procedures and a public page tracking past reports, updates, and future plans.

excerpt: RSP-2025: This update clarifies which Capability Thresholds would require enhanced safeguards beyond our current ASL-3 standards.
paraphrase: The March 2025 update clarifies which Capability Thresholds require safeguards beyond ASL-3.

excerpt: New Capability Thresholds: We have added a new capability threshold related to CBRN development, which defines capabilities that could substantially uplift the development capabilities of moderately resourced state programs.
paraphrase: A new CBRN-related capability threshold was added covering substantial uplift of moderately resourced state programs.

excerpt: We have also disaggregated our existing AI R&D capability thresholds, separating them into two distinct levels (the ability to fully automate entry-level AI research work, and the ability to cause dramatic acceleration in the rate of effective scaling) and provided additional detail on the corresponding Required Safeguards.
paraphrase: AI R&D thresholds were split into two distinct levels—full automation of entry-level research and dramatic scaling acceleration—with more detail on corresponding Required Safeguards.

excerpt: Iterative Commitment: We have adopted a general commitment to reevaluate our Capability Thresholds whenever we upgrade to a new set of Required Safeguards.
paraphrase: Anthropic committed to reevaluating Capability Thresholds each time Required Safeguards are upgraded.

excerpt: We have decided not to maintain a commitment to define ASL-N+1 evaluations by the time we develop ASL-N models; such an approach would add unnecessary complexity because Capability Thresholds do not naturally come grouped in discrete levels.
paraphrase: Anthropic dropped the commitment to predefine next-level evaluations, since Capability Thresholds are not naturally grouped in discrete levels.

excerpt: We believe it is more practical and sensible instead to commit to reconsidering the whole list of Capability Thresholds whenever we upgrade our safeguards.
paraphrase: Anthropic finds it more practical to reconsider the entire Capability Threshold list whenever safeguards are upgraded.

excerpt: ASL-3 Security: This update excludes both sophisticated insiders and state-compromised insiders from the ASL-3 Security Standard. Previously, only "highly sophisticated state-compromised insiders" were explicitly excluded.
paraphrase: The May 2025 update broadens exclusions from the ASL-3 Security Standard to cover both sophisticated insiders and state-compromised insiders, versus only highly sophisticated state-compromised insiders before.

excerpt: The model capabilities and threat models corresponding with the ASL-3 Security Standard do not warrant protection against either group: the CBRN-3 threat models entail large numbers of users having access to unguarded models (which is more likely to occur through a universal jailbreak than via model theft),
paraphrase: The rationale is that CBRN-3 threat models involve many users accessing unguarded models more likely via jailbreak than theft, so protection against these insider groups is not warranted.

excerpt: and the relatively small number of employees who might be capable of model theft does not significantly affect the risk level.
paraphrase: The small number of employees capable of model theft does not meaningfully change the risk level.

excerpt: For AI R&D-4, the threat models generally do not depend on model weight theft and instead entail AI systems engaging in autonomous internal sabotage.
paraphrase: For AI R&D-4, threat models rely on autonomous internal sabotage rather than weight theft.
